tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (arena_benchmark.cpp at the repo root, timing malloc/free, new[]/delete[] and obstack on the same allocation and free sequences), and the README states gcc-4.5.3 with CFLAGS -O2, glibc-2.14.1, Linux 3.4 and the CPU (Intel Atom N450 1.6 GHz). Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all present, so this is tier A (upgraded from C).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single thread (514,000 ops): obstack 272 ms vs malloc/free 26,882 ms vs new/delete 27,654 ms; 2 threads (538,000 ops): 162 ms vs 73,787 ms vs 90,000 ms; 4 threads (540,000 ops): 125 ms vs 108,245 ms vs 108,809 ms
corrections.baseline: malloc/free and new/delete (glibc-2.14.1, gcc-4.5.3 libstdc++, Linux 3.4)
corrections.caveats: Arena (bump/stack-style) allocator versus general-purpose malloc, so semantics differ; the timing excludes allocating the arena itself, and each thread gets its own arena while malloc threads share the glibc heap. Chunks run from 1 B to 4 MB, so glibc mmap/munmap of large blocks probably dominates the baseline time. 2012-era Atom netbook, gcc-4.5.3 and glibc-2.14.1; the author calls the results preliminary. Abandoned since 2015.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly; I added the 2-thread row. Metadata checked on github.com: BSL-1.0 (LICENSE_1_0.txt), 95 stars, not archived, last commit 2015-01-06.

tier_reason: First-party numbers, given in the README image alt text, against dlmalloc, buddy-alloc and umm_malloc on an STM32F401. The benchmark code is public (crates/rlsf_benchmark_farcri, using FarCri.rs), but no compiler version or flags are stated, so it cannot be A.

corrections.caveats: Numbers appear only as image alt text in the README; the charts are hosted on yvt.jp. Baseline dlmalloc is not in the list, and there is no comparison to glibc malloc, jemalloc or mimalloc; the README itself says modern allocators may beat it in allocation-heavy apps and that it does not support concurrent access. wee_alloc could not be timed (out of memory), and the wasm wee_alloc build used a fork. Compiler version and flags not stated. Benchmark crate: crates/rlsf_benchmark_farcri.

notes: README footnotes read: the latency figures were measured on an STM32F401 with FarCri.rs, and the latest version of each library was used. Metadata from github.com: MIT/Apache-2.0, 127 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-07-26.

tier_reason: First-party callgrind instruction counts against mimalloc v2.4.5, jemalloc and glibc, with bench scripts in the repo (bench/icount-arms.sh, bench/opscan.sh), plus wasm and ESP32-S3 timings. The x86 CPU model and the compiler and flags for the Linux runs are not stated, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Allocator-only instructions 0.52x / 0.81x / 0.83x of mimalloc on lua / perl / sqlite; whole program 0.96 / 0.99 / 1.00 vs mimalloc, 0.84 / 0.89 / 0.98 vs jemalloc, 0.81 / 0.81 / 0.99 vs glibc malloc; wasm32 churn 4.9-7.3x faster than dlmalloc (but a 2048 B tight loop runs 0.55-0.83x as fast); ESP32-S3 1.44-3.94x faster than esp-alloc 0.11
corrections.caveats: First-party only, and the repo is very new (commits since 2026-09-12, 3 stars). Instruction counts, not wall time; the whole-program lead over mimalloc is under 5% and sqlite is 1.00. CPU model and compiler flags for the x86 runs not stated; the lua count is not repeatable. It loses on a 2048 B tight loop in wasm (0.55-0.83x of dlmalloc). On ESP32-S3 it needs a 64 KiB RAM floor vs 8 KiB, returned 357 NULLs in 50,000 churn allocations vs 0, and refuses 64 KiB-aligned requests. The '54,914 active installs' figure is unverified marketing. It is a pure-Rust reimplementation of mimalloc (C mimalloc ships as a dev-only oracle). Bench scripts not run.

notes: The README tables match the record; I added the glibc whole-program row, widened the ESP32 range to the table's 1.44-3.94x, and added the wasm loss. It reimplements mimalloc in Rust, so the orchestrator may want to judge whether it folds as a mimalloc port (duplicate) or stands as its own entry.
